topic: American Airlines Flight 191: The DC-10 Engine Separation Mystery
niche_fit: yes - documented aviation disaster with NTSB investigation into unanswered mechanical failure questions
_transcript: On the 25th of May, 1979, American Airlines  flight 191 began rolling down the runway   for takeoff. The scheduled flight was due to  take around five hours… but would, in fact,   be in the air for just under a minute before  disaster struck. Flight 191 would soon end in   the worst single-aircraft aviation disaster  ever to take place in the United States. American Airlines, founded in 1930, is the  flag carrier airline of the United States.   Over the course of its lifetime, it has become the  largest passenger-carrying airline in the world. Beginning in the early 1970s, American  Airlines started working to maximize   the capacity of their long distance routes,  looking to both Boeing and McDonnell Douglas   for a solution. After seeing the results of both  the Boeing 747 and the McDonnel Douglas DC-10,   American Airlines would go on to select  the DC-10 as their premier jetliner. The DC-10’s of American Airlines had a long  and storied career – one that was not without   incident. In 1972, shortly after delivery, a  DC-10 flying as Flight 96 experienced a cargo   door blowout but was able to return safely with  no loss of life. However, this same issue would   be the cause of a major disaster on Turkish  Airlines Flight 981 just two years later. This accident would, unfortunately,  not be the last to involve a DC-10. On the 25th of May, 1979, American Airlines flight  191 was scheduled to take off from Chicago’s   O’Hare International Airport, bound for Los  Angeles International Airport. The trip was   expected to take only five hours. On board  the flight were 271 people – 258 passengers   and 13 crew. The cockpit crew consisted of  fifty-three-year-old Captain Walter Lux,   forty-nine-year-old First Officer James  Dillard, and fifty-six-year-old Flight   Engineer Alfred Udovich. All three men  were highly experienced airline pilots,   and would be flying a route they  had flown many times previously. At 3:04 PM, clearance was given for takeoff, and  first Officer Dillard set the throttles to takeoff   speed. The aircraft rolled down runway 32R,  gaining speed until it reached over 100 knots, and   then reached “V1” – the speed at which aborting  the takeoff was no longer safely possible. Captain Lux called out “rotate”, and First Officer  Dillard pulled the control column back to lift the   plane. At this exact moment, there was a shudder  that reverberated throughout the aircraft and a   metallic snapping sound. Captain Lux said only one  word - “Damn” – before the instruments went dead. In the control tower, an Air Traffic Controller  looked up in time to witness a shocking sight:   the left engine on Flight 191 had separated  from the aircraft and slammed into the runway.   He provided a shouted report to others in the  tower, then immediately called for emergency   equipment to be deployed. He attempted to  communicate with the stricken aircraft: “Flight American 1… 91 Heavy, you  wanna come back, and to what runway?” There was no reply. Soon, both those on the ground and in the tower  could see the plane begin to bank to the left,   before rolling fully onto its left side.  This event was captured by two different   photographers, who happened  to be watching at the time. Next, the plane began to fall back to the ground,  still on its side, until it slammed into a hanger   used as a car shop. The explosion and  fire that followed were both enormous,   with some eyewitnesses describing it as  resembling, “a rain of fire falling down…” Rescue teams quickly reached the site, and  were initially under the impression that   the nearby Standard Oil Petroleum Plant  was ablaze. It quickly became apparent,   instead, that a commercial jet had crashed.  Firefighters brought the flames under control,   and then began to look for survivors. It  was, however, soon very clear that no one   was left alive in the scattered debris. All  271 people on board were killed. Additionally,   two car mechanics, who had been at work  inside the hangar at the time of the crash,   were also killed. The burning debris from the  crash set fire to a trailer park behind the   airport, and caused considerable damage,  but no further deaths on the ground. The crash of Flight 191 was  at the time, and still is,   the most deadly single aircraft  accident in US aviation history. The National Transportation Safety Board (or  NTSB) began an investigation. From the start,   it was clear that the engine had  separated from the rest of the plane,   and that this had caused the aircraft to crash…  but there were still questions that remained: How and why did the engine separate? Had  it ever been possible for the pilots to   save the plane? And, most pertinently,  who was responsible for the accident? The Federal Aviation Administration (or  FAA) ordered that all DC-10s be grounded,   and any foreign-operated DC-10s not be allowed  to enter US airspace. Soon, pictures of the   doomed flight appeared in newspapers across  the country. These two events coincided to   cause public perception of the safety record of  the DC-10 to sharply decline. In the months that   followed, many passengers all over the world  would avoid any flight that used a DC-10. At first, the cause of the engine  separation was thought to be a   fractured bolt found on the runway.  This theory was announced at a press   conference… before the root cause was later  found not to be related to the damaged bolt. To find the true cause of the disaster,  investigators turned their attention to   the black boxes on the aircraft, both of  which yielded problematic results. The   Cockpit Voice Recorder cut out right after  Captian Lux’s exclamation of, “Damn”. It   had been powered by the left engine, and so had  lost power at the moment the engine separated. The Flight Data Recorder, on the other  hand, produced information that was   scrambled and difficult to interpret because of  the aircraft’s extreme and unnatural flight path. Further scrutiny of the engine found several  dents that had not been caused by the impact   onto the runway. Following this lead, it was found  that the aircraft, and specifically the engine,   had undergone maintenance at the American  Airlines Maintenance Facility in Tulsa,   Oklahoma two months prior to the crash. This  was part of a C-Check – a routine, comprehensive   inspection of systems on board an aircraft,  usually scheduled every twelve to eighteen months. Investigation of the Maintenance Facility  lead to a troubling discovery. It was found   that maintenance personnel had not been  following the standard guidelines for   repairing an engine. Instead of detaching the  engine from its support, known as a pylon,   for maintenance, they were taking off  the entire engine assembly with the   pylon attached. After maintenance was complete,  it would then be reattached using a forklift. This crude method of reattachment could cause  the pylon to become improperly aligned with its   locking pins, resulting in the pins being bent.  On top of this, it was easy to accidentally slam   the pylon into place, damaging it and  creating microscopic stress fractures. It was not only American Airlines personnel  who were using this shortcut. The staff of   Continental Airlines were also routinely  detaching and reattaching engines using the   same method. With the DC-10 grounding still  in effect, emergency repairs were enacted   across the fleets of both airlines. Many  planes were found to have stress fractures,   some of which were dangerously  close to expanding into a breakage. With the root cause now determined, the actions  of the pilots were scrutinized. There was some   speculation that they could have returned to  the airport without incident. Aircraft that   are certified in commercial aviation are  designed to be able to fly using only one   engine in an emergency. Flight 191 still  had two working engines when it crashed. While it may never be known with absolute  certainty what happened on the flight,   the QRH, or Quick Reference Handbook, did  shed some light on what most likely happened. In the event of an engine failure,  the QRH instructed pilots to slow   their speed ready for an emergency  landing. In the case of this accident,   there was no way for the flight crew to  know they had physically lost an engine and   therefore should have instead maintained speed  to keep the aircraft aerodynamically balanced. In photographs taken right before impact,  a trail of white mist is visible. This   was found to be hydraulic fluid. The loss of  hydraulic fluid would have caused the flaps   and slats on the left side of the plane to  revert to a neutral position. With the right   flaps and slats positioned to slow the plane  down, the imbalance in airflow and lack of   speed would have easily caused the plane  to enter a stall, and roll onto its side. One final question that emerged was, why  didn’t the crew know they were stalling?   This was answered by the loss of the Cockpit Voice  Recorder. It was not the only system linked to the   left engine of the plane. So too was the Captain’s  “stick shaker” (or stall warning system). At the time, it was not required that both  control columns be equipped with stick shakers,   or that power for the stick shakers was to be  drawn from all engines. The option to have both   control columns equipped with stick shakers was  offered by the manufacturer McDonnell Douglas,   but American Airlines had opted out. The NTSB concluded that the simplified,  non-recommended maintenance procedure   carried out by American Airlines  was the root cause of the disaster,   and that the flight crew had acted appropriately  given their knowledge of the situation. American Airlines was fined $500,000  (the equivalent of $1.6 million today)   and orders were issued by the FAA,  at the recommendation of the NTSB,   that more strict protocols be enforced on  airlines regarding aircraft maintenance. It was   also mandated that electrical systems be powered  by all engines on a given aircraft, not just one. In addition to this, both the pilot  and co-pilot were now required to   have stick shakers, and automatic  safety valves were to be fitted on   hydraulic lines to prevent a loss of  pressure should they become severed. The FAA was heavily criticized for its  lax monitoring of airline maintenance   practices. The crew chief who supervised the  aircraft during its final inspection before   the disaster – a man named Earl Russell  Marshall – would later take his own life. American Airlines continued to  use the DC-10 until the year 2000,   around which time it was displaced by newer  and more efficient jets. The location of the   disaster would remain unused until  2011, when a permanent memorial was   constructed. O’Hare International Airport  remains a bustling airport to this day,   but it is one that is forever remembered as the  location where 271 passengers lost their lives.
